seo.title: 5 LeetCode Mediums — Spotting The Pattern From The Words Alone
altTitles: Five Problems, One Method (DSA Pattern Dojo, Finale)
How To Pick The Right Pattern Under Interview Pressure
seo.hook: Five problems. Name the pattern before the code.
seo.breakdown: five real interview problems, each one solved by reading the signal words first
queries: how to identify pattern from problem statement
search in rotated sorted array solution

scenes.narration: Five problems you've never seen. Ten patterns you have. Which one, and how fast can you tell?
Ten patterns are behind us here in the NBX Studio Dojo. Now five real interview problems, and the only thing that matters is how we choose.

Same routine for every one of these. Read the statement. Circle the signal words. Name the pattern those words point at. Then check the core idea really applies, rather than just sounding right. And only then write anything. Watch how short step three gets once step two is done properly. That's the whole promise of learning patterns rather than memorising solutions.

dsaFramework.headline: The method, in [one screen]
dsaFramework.caption: what we do five times
dsaFramework.premise: The six-step method, the one we run on every problem that follows.

scenes.narration: An array of heights, each one a vertical line. Find the two lines that hold the most water between them. Circle the words. Two. Maximum. A pair of elements. An array. Two and pair together point straight at two pointers. But there's a catch worth noticing: this array isn't sorted, and sorted was our signal last time. So does the pattern still hold?

dsaSignals.headline: One · [Container With Most Water]
dsaSignals.caption: reading the statement
dsaSignals.problem: Given an array of heights, where each value is a vertical line, find the two lines that together with the x-axis hold the most water. Return that maximum area.

scenes.narration: It does hold, and the reasoning is worth having. Start at the widest possible container: one line at each end. The area is the shorter of the two heights, multiplied by the distance between them, because water spills over the lower side. Now move the shorter line inward. Moving the taller one can never help, since the shorter side is what caps the volume and the width only shrinks. Order of n, constant space, and no sorting needed, because the elimination argument here's about height rather than order.

dsaPtrs.headline: Yes, and [here is why]
dsaPtrs.caption: the widest container first
dsaPtrs.premise: Container With Most Water. Each box is the height of a vertical line; two pointers start at the outermost pair.

lines.detail: Water spills over the lower side.
Move the SHORTER line. The taller one cannot help.

scenes.narration: Find the length of the longest substring with no repeating characters. Circle them. Longest. Substring, not subsequence, and that distinction is the whole question. Without repeating, which is a rule the answer has to keep obeying. Substring means contiguous, and contiguous plus a rule is a sliding window, the variable kind that grows and shrinks rather than the fixed kind that slides.

dsaSignals.headline: Two · [Longest Substring]
dsaSignals.caption: reading the statement
dsaSignals.problem: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeating characters.

scenes.narration: A set holds the characters currently inside the window. The right edge moves forward, adding a character each time and growing the window. The window never restarts, which is the whole trick, and when a duplicate turns up the left edge moves in, dropping characters until the duplicate is gone and the rule holds again. Every character is added once and removed at most once, so it's order of n even though both pointers move. Neither pointer ever walks backwards, and that is the property to say out loud.

dsaWindow.headline: Grow, then [shrink]
dsaWindow.caption: the window repairs itself
dsaWindow.premise: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Each box is one character of the string, and the frame is the window we are still allowed to keep.

lines.detail: What is currently inside the window.
Grow from the right, one character at a time.
Duplicate: shrink from the left until it is gone.

scenes.narration: A sorted array was rotated at some pivot. Find a target, and do it in log n time. Sorted. Rotated. Search. And order log n, stated outright in the constraints. That last one isn't a hint, it's an instruction: log n on an array means binary search and essentially nothing else. The interesting part is that rotation appears to break the precondition, so let's look at whether it really does.

dsaSignals.headline: Three · [Rotated Sorted Array]
dsaSignals.caption: reading the statement
dsaSignals.problem: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated at some unknown pivot. Given a target, return its index, or -1. You must do it in O(log n) time.

scenes.narration: Here's the insight it turns on. Cut a rotated array anywhere and one half is always still fully sorted. It can't be otherwise, because a single rotation puts one break point in, and a break point can only sit in one half. So compare mid with left to work out which half is the clean one. If the target sits inside that sorted half, search there; otherwise search the other. Still log n, because we're still throwing away half the array every step. Rotation looked like it broke the precondition, and it never did.

dsaBsearch.headline: One half is [always sorted]
dsaBsearch.caption: the insight
dsaBsearch.premise: Search in Rotated Sorted Array. Each box is a value; the row was sorted, then rotated, so one half of it is still in order.

lines.detail: Left half is the sorted one.
Target is inside it, so search there.
Otherwise the answer is in the other half.

scenes.narration: Your turn, and this is a real interview moment. A question says: find the minimum number of coins to make an amount. Which pattern? Greedy, take the biggest coin each time. Dynamic programming. Or backtracking, try everything. Have a think, and pause the video if you'd like a moment. Ready? Dynamic programming, and the reason is that greedy genuinely fails on this one. We'll see exactly how in a minute.

quiz.question: Fewest coins to make an amount. Which pattern?
quiz.why: Greedy fails on coin change. We are about to see it fail.

scenes.narration: A grid of ones and zeroes. Land and water. Count the islands. Circle them. Grid. Connected, or adjacent. Count the components. No shortest anywhere, which is interesting, because breadth-first search is still the natural tool here: we're using it to flood a region rather than to measure a distance. Depth-first would work just as well, and saying that out loud is worth marks.

dsaSignals.headline: Four · [Number of Islands]
dsaSignals.caption: reading the statement
dsaSignals.problem: Given a 2D grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands. An island is land connected horizontally or vertically.

scenes.narration: Walk the grid cell by cell. When you hit a piece of land nobody has visited, that's a new island, so add one to the count. The ring spreads until the island runs out. Then flood it: breadth-first search out from that cell, marking every connected piece of land as visited so nothing is counted twice. And the outer scan carries on from where it left off. Every cell is visited once, so the cost is rows times columns.

dsaGrid.headline: Flood, then [count]
dsaGrid.caption: one island at a time
dsaGrid.premise: Number of Islands. Each circle is a grid cell — 1 is land, 0 is water — and the badge is how far the flood has spread from where it started.

lines.detail: Scan the grid, cell by cell.

lines.text: if grid[r][c] == '1' and (r,c) not in seen:

lines.detail: Flood it, so it is never counted again.

scenes.narration: Coins of different values, and a total to reach. Return the fewest coins, or minus one if it can't be done. Circle them. Fewest, or minimum. Number of. Choices at every step, since any coin can be next. And subproblems that overlap, because the best way to make seven turns up inside the best way to make eight. Minimum, choices and overlap together mean dynamic programming. Those three together are the tell, every single time.

dsaSignals.headline: Five · [Coin Change]
dsaSignals.caption: reading the statement
dsaSignals.problem: Given coins of different denominations and a total amount, return the fewest coins needed to make that amount. If it cannot be made, return -1.

scenes.narration: A table where entry i holds the fewest coins needed to make amount i. Base case: zero coins make zero. Amount one, amount two, amount three, each solved once and then only read. And for every amount upward we try each coin and keep the best: one coin, plus whatever it costs to make the remainder. Amount times coins, which is a loop inside a loop and nothing worse.

dsaDp.headline: Build [upward]
dsaDp.caption: every amount, once
dsaDp.premise: Coin Change. Each box is an amount from 0 up to the target, and the number in it is the fewest coins that make that amount.

lines.detail: dp[i] = fewest coins to make amount i.
Zero coins make zero. The base case.
Build upward, one amount at a time.

lines.text: return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != inf else -1

scenes.narration: Here's why greedy is wrong, and it's worth memorising because it comes up. Coins of one, five and eleven, and you need fifteen. Greedy takes the biggest first: eleven, then four ones. Five coins. The real answer is three: five, five and five. Greedy failed because taking eleven stranded it, and greedy never reconsiders. Dynamic programming tries every coin at every amount, which is exactly the reconsidering greedy refuses to do.

dsaCost.headline: Why [greedy fails] here
dsaCost.caption: the counterexample to remember
dsaCost.premise: The same job priced two ways as the input grows: the obvious method against the pattern. Longer bar means more work.

scenes.narration: Here's what to actually do tomorrow. Do the four problems listed under each pattern, in the order given. Before you write anything, say the pattern out loud and why. When you're stuck for more than fifteen minutes, read the solution, then close it and write it from memory. And redo the ones you got wrong a week later, because recognition fades fast.

Three things from the whole series. The words in the question carry the pattern, and reading properly beats coding quickly. Ten patterns cover most of what gets asked, which is a much smaller job than it looks from the outside. And saying your reasoning out loud is the thing being graded.

points.text: Ten patterns cover most of it
